title: Protect brain tissue during acute ischemic stroke

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a rapidly deliverable treatment that preserves threatened, still-viable brain tissue during an acute ischemic stroke and produces lasting benefits in everyday function. The intended capability would work safely in a broad range of eligible patients, alongside restoration of blood flow when appropriate. Tissue protection would not automatically restore tissue that has already died.

Conceptual synthesis: the target is dependable protection despite the uncertainties of emergency stroke care, including uncertain onset time, different sites of arterial blockage, differences in remaining blood flow and concurrent treatments. The concept spans neurology, emergency medicine, vascular biology and pharmacology. No particular drug or protective mechanism is established as the solution by the supplied evidence.

significance.text: Conditional impact assessment: broad, safe preservation of threatened tissue, accompanied by durable functional benefit, could substantially reduce stroke disability and dependence on long-term care. Effectiveness when restoration of blood flow is delayed could extend that benefit to difficult treatment settings. Reduced mortality and protection during delayed reperfusion would each require direct demonstration; neither follows automatically from a smaller final infarct.

The revolutionary capability would be reliable clinical protection across heterogeneous patients and treatment circumstances. A narrow benefit in one selected population could still be valuable, but would establish a more limited achievement. Near-zero infarct size across all patients remains an aspirational upper bound, not a demonstrated result or a realistic promise established by this record. Impact would depend on treatment timing, stroke mechanism, remaining viable tissue and access to emergency care.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed capability gap: a treatment must preserve enough viable tissue to improve patients’ lasting function while remaining safe across a useful treatment window. The research frames injury as evolving with time and blood flow and interacting with reperfusion. These are coherent scientific considerations, but the supplied record contains no retained source passages supporting their detailed mechanisms or magnitude.

Engineering and clinical synthesis: concrete barriers include delivering effective protection quickly enough, identifying patients with salvageable tissue despite uncertain onset, accommodating different occlusion sites and blood-flow conditions, and avoiding harmful interactions with thrombolysis or thrombectomy. A convincing intervention must also translate tissue preservation into meaningful clinical outcomes. The relative importance of these barriers, and which mechanisms can overcome them, remain unspecified by the supplied evidence.

current_state.text: The supplied bibliography identifies a 2025 publication titled “Efficacy and safety of nerinetide in acute ischaemic stroke in patients undergoing endovascular thrombectomy without previous thrombolysis (ESCAPE-NEXT).” That title describes a specific treatment setting: patients undergoing thrombectomy without previous thrombolysis. It does not by itself establish effectiveness across other stroke populations, treatment combinations or delayed-reperfusion settings.

The reconciled research describes ESCAPE-NEXT as randomized and reports that 45% of nerinetide recipients and 46% of placebo recipients achieved the stated favorable functional outcome at 90 days. These figures are retained as an unverified report from the supplied research. The source index contains no captured abstract or article text, so the outcome definition, numerical comparison, randomization details and statistical interpretation could not be checked against retained content. The percentages alone do not establish equivalence or resolve whether benefit exists in other settings.

The research attributes its figures to an indexed abstract and says the publisher blocked full-article access during the earlier check. Neither the abstract nor evidence of that access restriction was retained, so those access claims remain unconfirmed. This limits interpretation of the reported result without showing that it is false. No bounded freshness search record was supplied to establish the broader state of neuroprotection as of November 1, 2026; the available material therefore neither demonstrates the proposed broad capability nor establishes conclusively that it remains unachieved across the field.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: large randomized trials in representative acute ischemic stroke populations should show substantially smaller final infarcts together with durable, clinically meaningful improvement in function, alongside standard reperfusion care where appropriate. Independent replication should establish that the benefit is reproducible. The supplied research also proposes improved survival; this is an ambitious additional outcome to demonstrate, rather than an established necessary definition of successful neuroprotection.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated substantial infarct reduction and durable clinically meaningful functional improvement

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: trials should identify effective treatment windows, eligible patient groups, adverse effects and interactions with concurrent therapies. They should distinguish benefit with timely reperfusion from benefit when reperfusion is delayed, and describe limits associated with uncertain onset, occlusion site and baseline tissue viability. Broad enrollment and consistent results would establish demonstrated breadth across the tested circumstances, not literal protection for every patient or reversal of already-dead tissue. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not established consensus thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Report effective treatment boundaries, safety, and dependence on reperfusion

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NRL-06, “Replace lost brain tissue while preserving learned function,” and NRL-05, “Regenerate a severely injured spinal cord with functional reconnection,” share the goal of reducing lasting neurological disability. Their central challenge is rebuilding or replacing damaged tissue and restoring function. NRL-13 instead seeks to preserve viable brain tissue during an acute event; successful protection could reduce subsequent repair needs without solving regeneration.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-10, “Safe, programmable delivery to selected cells throughout the human brain,” could overlap with delivering a protective intervention to its intended targets. Its broad delivery capability is distinct from proving rapid clinical protection during stroke, and the supplied record does not establish that such programmable delivery is necessary for NRL-13.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-09, “Prevent Alzheimer’s dementia before irreversible functional loss,” NRL-11, “Halt established Alzheimer’s disease and restore lost function,” and NRL-15, “Identify and treat shared mechanisms of neurodegeneration across diseases,” overlap with preserving neural function before irreversible loss. NRL-13 concerns an acute vascular emergency with different timing and treatment constraints. A protective effect in stroke would not by itself establish prevention or treatment of chronic neurodegenerative disease, or prove a shared mechanism.

change_log.change: Preserved the concept identity and expanded the explanation of broad, rapidly deliverable protection of viable tissue.
change_log.reason: The review supports a coherent candidate capability despite missing retained evidence; evidence gaps do not justify removing the concept.

change_log.change: Retained the reported 45% versus 46% 90-day outcomes while explicitly identifying them as unverified research reports.
change_log.reason: This preserves useful quantitative detail without implying that the absent abstract or article was inspected.

change_log.change: Qualified the reported randomization, indexed-abstract access and publisher blocking, and removed a definitive field-wide claim that neuroprotection remains unproven.
change_log.reason: The source index has no captured content, and no freshness search record establishes the broader state as of November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Separated functional benefit, infarct reduction, survival and effectiveness during delayed reperfusion.
change_log.reason: These are distinct outcomes; smaller infarcts do not automatically establish reduced mortality or benefit under delayed treatment.

change_log.change: Framed completion criteria as proposals and survival improvement as an ambitious additional target.
change_log.reason: The supplied material does not establish consensus thresholds or make improved survival necessary to every successful demonstration.

change_log.change: Integrated treatment heterogeneity, reperfusion compatibility, independent replication and limits of finite testing into the relevant sections.
change_log.reason: These distinctions explain the capability gap and the boundaries of a convincing demonstration without repeating review commentary.

change_log.change: Added relevant roster relationships while preserving distinctions between acute protection, regeneration, delivery and chronic disease treatment.
change_log.reason: Related capabilities may complement one another without being interchangeable or warranting merged entries.

unresolved_issues: The ESCAPE-NEXT abstract and full article were not captured. The reported outcome percentages, outcome definition, trial methods, statistical uncertainty and safety findings remain unverified against source content.
The earlier report of indexed-abstract access and publisher blocking cannot be confirmed from retained artifacts.
No supplied freshness search establishes the field-wide state of acute stroke neuroprotection as of November 1, 2026.

The review recommended replacing the numerical trial summary with a bibliographic-only account. That recommendation was adopted in substance by qualifying the evidence, but not by deleting the figures: the user requested preservation of unresolved quantitative detail, and the review identifies missing verification rather than contradictory evidence.

The supplied evidence does not determine which protective mechanism, treatment window or patient population could support broad clinical success, or whether mortality reduction and benefit during delayed reperfusion are achievable.

brief.title: Saving threatened brain tissue during a stroke
possible: Someone having a stroke caused by a blocked artery could receive a rapid treatment to keep threatened brain tissue alive. It would work alongside treatment to restore blood flow when appropriate, helping preserve the person’s ability to function in everyday life.
why: Lasting protection could mean less disability after a stroke and less dependence on long-term care. Protection that works even when blood flow cannot be restored promptly could also help people in difficult treatment settings.

sources.showed: ESCAPE-NEXT is a clinical trial of nerinetide in stroke patients undergoing mechanical clot removal without first receiving clot-dissolving medicine.
sources.cited_for: It examines a candidate protective treatment alongside mechanical clot removal in a specific patient group.
sources.not_established: It does not establish dependable protection across different stroke populations, treatment combinations or delays in restoring blood flow.

shown: ESCAPE-NEXT studied nerinetide in people having a clot mechanically removed who had not first received clot-dissolving medicine. This tests a specific treatment setting; dependable tissue protection with lasting everyday benefits across a broad range of patients remains to be demonstrated.
missing: A treatment must reproducibly save threatened tissue and deliver lasting, meaningful improvements in everyday function.
Protection must reach patients quickly enough and work safely across a useful treatment window.
Trials must establish which patients benefit and how protection interacts with treatments that restore blood flow.
Benefit when blood flow is restored late, and any reduction in deaths, require direct demonstration.

milestones.label: Repeated trials show less brain damage and lasting functional benefit
milestones.explanation: Large randomized trials would have to show substantially less dead brain tissue and meaningful, lasting functional improvement, with independent replication. This would establish that protection reliably helps patients.

milestones.label: Trials establish when protection works and remains safe
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to establish treatment windows, eligible patients, harms and interactions, including whether benefit depends on prompt restoration of blood flow. This would define where treatment can reliably help.

uncertain: Which protective mechanism can work across different blockage sites, remaining blood flow and amounts of still-living tissue?
How much benefit is possible when stroke onset is uncertain or restoration of blood flow is delayed?
What size of tissue reduction and functional improvement should count as substantial, reproducible protection?

page.title: Pharmacological cerebroprotection for acute ischemic stroke
page.definition: A drug preserves threatened brain tissue during acute ischemic stroke, brain injury caused by an arterial blockage, and improves lasting function. US approval specifies the eligible population and treatment conditions, including use with reperfusion, the restoration of blood flow.

goal.need: ESCAPE-NEXT randomized 850 adults undergoing thrombectomy without previous thrombolysis. At 90 days, functional independence (modified Rankin Scale score 0–2) occurred in 206/454 nerinetide recipients (45%) and 181/396 placebo recipients (46%): adjusted odds ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.72–1.30; p=0.82. Nerinetide did not improve this outcome; the control group quantifies disability remaining after thrombectomy.

statements.quote: The overall goal is to determine whether such interventions can significantly improve outcome compared to reperfusion alone
statements.context: RFA-NS-22-033 describes preclinical cerebroprotective interventions given before or during reperfusion.

statements.quote: Confirmatory pivotal studies based on the secondary analyses or preliminary efficacy of compounds, including nerinetide, uric acid, edaravone-dexborneol, and ApTOLL
statements.context: Section 4.11 lists this research need; its current recommendation advises against neuroprotective treatment to improve functional outcome.

completion.title: FDA approves a cerebroprotective drug to improve functional outcome after acute ischemic stroke.
completion.criterion: FDA issues marketing approval for a drug whose acute ischemic stroke indication establishes functional benefit from cerebroprotection, with the population and conditions of use specified in its labeling. Under 21 CFR 314.105(c), FDA must determine that the drug meets statutory standards for safety and effectiveness, manufacturing and controls, and labeling. A positive trial or an accepted application does not itself constitute this approval.
completion.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 314.105(a) and (c).
completion.threshold_quote: the drug meets the statutory standards for safety and effectiveness, manufacturing and controls, and labeling
completion.basis: An indication-specific approval provides an externally adjudicated safety-and-effectiveness test. This completion boundary is US authorization for the labeled stroke population and treatment conditions; it does not assert efficacy across every stroke setting. The FDA regulation specifies no universal minimum infarct reduction or modified Rankin Scale effect.

milestones.title: A cerebroprotective drug reduces brain tissue damage and improves behavior in an animal stroke model.
milestones.criterion: A candidate demonstrates beneficial effects on both tissue damage and behavior in experimental ischemic stroke, the qualification result specified by STAIR XI. In 2018, ApTLR#4FT given after permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion reduced cortical injury and improved stride length at 21 days in mice; the histology and behavioral comparisons used n=10 per group.
milestones.set_by: STAIR XI expert consensus, Table 2A, Histological and behavioral outcomes row (2021).
milestones.threshold_quote: Beneficial effects can be demonstrated using measures of behavior and tissue damage

milestones.title: A cerebroprotectant establishes human exposure and tolerability sufficient for phase 2 testing.
milestones.criterion: Human dosing yields pharmacokinetic and pharmacological information sufficient to design controlled phase 2 studies, as specified by the FDA phase 1 definition. ApTOLL was tested in 46 healthy men from June 18, 2019, through March 20, 2020, with single intravenous doses of 0.7–70 mg and a repeated-dose cohort. No serious adverse events were reported; mean plasma half-life was 9.3 hours. Follow-up extended to 15 days after dosing.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.21(a)(1), phase 1 development criterion; ApTOLL provides a Spanish trial example.
milestones.threshold_quote: to permit the design of well-controlled, scientifically valid, Phase 2 studies.

milestones.title: 3K3A-APC reaches a dose with estimated dose-limiting toxicity of at most 10% in stroke patients.
milestones.criterion: RHAPSODY identifies the highest tested 3K3A-APC dose with estimated protocol-defined dose-limiting toxicity of ≤10%, assessed until 48 hours after the last dose, in patients receiving alteplase, thrombectomy or both. Its randomized phase 2 study enrolled 110 patients: 66 received 3K3A-APC and 44 placebo. The maximum tolerated dose was 540 μg/kg per infusion, with estimated toxicity of 7%. This was a dose-finding result, not demonstrated functional efficacy.
milestones.set_by: NIH NeuroNEXT RHAPSODY investigators, NCT02222714; this numerical safety criterion was defined specifically for 3K3A-APC.
milestones.threshold_quote: We defined the MTD as the highest study dose with an estimated dose limiting toxicity (DLT) rate of ≤10%.

milestones.title: Loberamisal improves 90-day modified Rankin Scale 0–1 outcomes in a phase 3 trial at two-sided α=0.05.
milestones.criterion: LAIS tests loberamisal 40 mg intravenously daily for 10 days against placebo plus standard care, started ≤48 hours after onset in adults aged 18–80 years with National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale scores 7–20 and prestroke mRS ≤1. Success is a higher proportion with mRS 0–1 at 90 days at two-sided α=0.05. Published September 10, 2026: 998 randomized, 997 treated; 350/502 (69.7%) versus 279/495 (56.3%), risk ratio 1.24 (95% CI 1.12–1.36); serious adverse events 43/502 versus 53/495. The trial involved 32 hospitals in China.
milestones.set_by: LAIS investigators, NCT06517173, published phase 3 protocol; the endpoint and population were specified for loberamisal.
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary outcome is proportion of patients achieving mRS 0–1 at 90 days.

milestones.title: FDA accepts a new drug application for an acute-stroke cerebroprotectant for substantive review.
milestones.criterion: FDA files a new drug application for the cerebroprotective acute ischemic stroke indication after determining that the application is sufficiently complete for substantive review. Under 21 CFR 314.101(a), the filing determination occurs within 60 days of receipt and FDA notifies the applicant in writing. The milestone requires acceptance for filing, not the developer's submission alone.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 314.101(a)(1)–(2).
milestones.threshold_quote: the NDA is sufficiently complete to permit a substantive review.

not_found: No field-wide numerical definition of protection across all onset times, occlusion sites and reperfusion settings was found in STAIR, AHA/ASA or NINDS documents.
No FDA filing acceptance or approval specifically for pharmacological cerebroprotection in acute ischemic stroke was located.
The supplied ScienceDirect ESCAPE-NEXT page returned an access error; its published abstract was accessible through PubMed.
